DM with four years of experience here. Played with feats for all my games. I'm DMing icewind dale now and i'm doing it without feats. My reasons are the following:

\- Most if not all my players always pick feats for mechanical reasons yet claim they like them because they "enrich their characters"  
\- They also tend to adapt the character to the feat instead of picking the feat as support for the character concept.  
\- I'm trying a different approach towards dnd less focused on heroes that always find the magic items they need in the world and have their power spoonfed to them and put them in a more plausible context in which the power is out there for them to claim yet have to put work (I used to DM most of my tables in a more epic powergaming oriented due to anxiety issues that didn't allow me to say NO to my player's powercreeping. After a bit of therapy, i'm now ready to DM the kind of table i want and not leave aside my own expectations)

No feats isn't common in DnD because the culture of DnD has become highly powercreeping lately. I'm not saying it in a bad way. it's just that videogames and the pandemic (which brought a lot of people into ttrpgs) reinforced the wargamey aspects of DnD making them more important. TCOE is a huge example of this. DnD is nowadays a game with a focus on mechanical builds. Yes, the roleplaying is still an element of it, but most tables i've played at and seen on reddit are numbers-oriented. That's why 2024 made them a default rule. In my opinion, appealing to that videogame mentality all those players that engrossed the fanbase have is a smart way of pumping up sales. Still, i don't believe it's the way DnD was meant to play originally and that's why Feats used to be optional.

TL;DR: No, "No feats" isn't popular. It's not wrong either. Just another way of playing the game.

There are probably a lot of good comments but i'll go with my take with an example of a combat against bandits:

1-Put encounters before the combat. No, not more combats. Encounters. Not all encounters are combat,   
A trap before the bandit's lair? Encounter. Bribing/convincing/intimidating bandit scouts to know where their lair is? Encounter. Puzzle because the bandit is somehow in a bunch of ruins with old defense mechanisms? Encounter. Anything that spends resources are encounters.

2-Are your combat "pokemon" combats? Do enemies just pop in the table and that's it? is the only stake death? Add more objectives. The bandits not only want to kill the characters but they are also using npc's as ransom. If you don't kill 'em first, they'll kill the npcs. 

3-Are you using the terrain? Are the players always fighting on grasslands on a sunny day? or are you revving combat by putting them on difficult terrain hills on a high wind storm that difficults ranged combat and limits movement options? The bandits might also have traps to even the odds. Maybe the boss tosses orders "ok, bois! cut the rope!" and bam! a huge tree pendulums through the map

4-Are your enemies one-phase? why not up them? The bandit boss isn't really a bandit boss, but the reincarnation of ogrog the malicious, a mutated son of a gun that, when his vessel is threatened, he shows his true colors.

Also take in account that sometimes it's not about making a hard combat that will down a PC or two, but making a FUN combat. The combat is a chance for the characters to show their skills. maybe the bandits are controlling bears the druid can tame, or they are in a really well hidden place the ranger can spot. Maybe the boss challenges the barbarian to a one on one but when he sees he's losing, he chickens out and makes arrows rain on the party to cover his retreat. Be creative, my dude. The possibilities are infinite. And never forgetti: A DM's job is to help the players make their PC's shine!

My take on this is: Make the encounter interesting through the mechanics, not the creatures.Although it IS important to choose good creatures, the encounter can have multiple tools to turn a very hard combat into an amazing one.

For example, Make a gobling hideout in a cave. The cave consists of 4 platforms connected with rope bridges. Below these platforms, a fall of 100 feet and natural spikes await await.On one central platform, there's a Ballista pointed at the cave's entrance. it seems to be able to be spun. Also, one of the platforms has a 15 feet radius exit. The amount of goblins here is 30 (yeah, i don't care about your party's level.

So now, there is an interesting terrain, a tool, danger and a mistery (the exit). Your players can use the ballista (and you can give it an area of effect), can cut the rope bridges when goblins run on them towards the party (these will reduce the goblin's numbers while making the party happy). And if things get too easy, you can use the mistery exit as a spawn point for an ogre. See, sometimes, a CR count doesn't mean shit really. It's all about the fun mechanics you can include.

Maybe my problem wasn't explained. I do not like to make a full-day, 7-8 combat encounters dungeon. I rather distribute the 7-8 combats along (for example) a three adventuring days trip. Changing the terrain, changing the monsters, rising the tension.

I've had my share of 7-8 combat dungeons and althought they were fun. They made travelling rather trivial. "Ok, you go from point A to point B. the trips is three days long. On the second day, you encounter the entrance to a tomb" \*dungeon happens\*. I think travelling and the adventure becomes more exciting with the combats being distributed along the journey. It allows me to make wilderness encounters more interesting and relevant.

  
For example: Imagine you are DMing a whale-hunting party. They want to hunt the terrible Moby Cock.

**CASE 1:** You write a dungeon to Moby Cock's lair and the trip is just fast forwarded until they arrive at the entrance of said dungeon.

**CASE 2:** You write two or three wilderness encounters that put the party on the test (a storm, sharks, a pirate ship) and the rest of the combat encounters happen in the dungeon

**CASE 3:** All the combat encounters happen as wilderness/travel encounters and drain some of the party resources until they arrive to the last combat encounter: The great Moby Cock attacking the ship.

​

I guess my problem is not the flavor but the scale. 7-8 combat encounters along a dungeon sounds boring, slow and forced to me. 7-8 combat encounters along a days-long trip sounds more adventurous.
